name: dr evil pinky
message: Use for a smug, knowingly mischievous reaction when an idea is devious, tempting, or suspiciously convenient.
relational_pattern: A speaker recognizes an appealingly devious possibility and signals quiet scheming rather than open menace.
example_context: A coworker suggests scheduling the difficult meeting for a day the manager is away, and you reply with this to acknowledge the crafty workaround.
near_miss_context: Your friend directly threatens to hurt someone; the playful scheming tone would trivialize a serious threat.

name: Expectation vs Reality
message: Use when an advertisement, listing, photo, or confident promise creates an ideal picture that the disappointing real result immediately contradicts.
relational_pattern: A polished advertised version is compared with the cramped, shabby, awkward, or ordinary thing someone actually receives.
example_context: The rental listing shows a huge bright kitchen, but arrival reveals one dim room, a hot plate, and a parking-lot window.
near_miss_context: Avoid when the delivered place or result substantially matches what the photos and promise showed.

name: Monkey looking away
message: Use when someone awkwardly avoids eye contact after being implicated, caught, contradicted, or reminded of their own behavior.
relational_pattern: Attention is deliberately redirected away from an uncomfortable fact that applies to the person reacting.
example_context: In a group chat, someone complains about late replies immediately after leaving everyone on read for a week; answer with this reaction.
near_miss_context: A friend misses the conversation because they are genuinely focused on an urgent phone call, not evading an embarrassing point.

name: Gabe - shut up about the sun
message: Use when an overrepeated topic has exhausted everyone and somebody finally demands that it stop.
relational_pattern: Persistent fixation by one person provokes an exasperated shutdown from another.
example_context: Your roommate mentions their new air fryer for the tenth time that evening, so the group sends this to end the running commentary.
near_miss_context: A teammate brings up a safety defect for the first time; shutting them down would not match the accumulated annoyance.

name: Young Thug and Lil Durk troubleshooting
message: Use for two people intensely examining a confusing problem together, often with more determination than expertise.
relational_pattern: Partners jointly inspect an unclear situation and improvise a diagnosis.
example_context: You and a coworker stare at a spreadsheet formula neither of you wrote, so you post this as your troubleshooting status.
near_miss_context: One engineer already knows the exact fix and applies it alone without discussion; there is no shared puzzlement.

name: Never give up
message: Use to encourage continued effort when repeated setbacks make success look unlikely but not impossible.
relational_pattern: Persistence is framed as continuing to reach for a goal despite successive near-failures.
example_context: A friend has been rejected from several internships but is preparing another strong application, and you send this as encouragement.
near_miss_context: Someone keeps gambling after serious losses with no plan or limit; celebrating persistence would endorse harmful escalation.

name: Jump on Rake
message: Use to compare an ordinary mistake with a much more elaborate way of causing the same failure to oneself.
relational_pattern: A simple self-own is escalated into spectacular, unnecessary self-sabotage.
example_context: A friend could admit they forgot a deadline but instead invents an elaborate excuse that creates three new problems; label the two approaches with this.
near_miss_context: Two options lead to genuinely different outcomes, so presenting one as merely the flashier version of the same blunder would be misleading.

name: salt bae
message: Use when someone adds a stylish finishing touch, an extra flourish, or a conspicuously small contribution to something already complete.
relational_pattern: A minor addition is performed with outsized theatrical confidence.
example_context: After a teammate finishes the entire presentation, you add one emoji to the title slide and jokingly post this as your contribution.
near_miss_context: You quietly correct a fundamental error that changes the whole project; that is substantive work, not decorative seasoning.

name: Cute cat hehe and not hehe
message: Use when something initially seems funny but a second thought, new detail, or personal implication abruptly kills the laughter.
relational_pattern: Amusement reverses into discomfort once the joke's consequence becomes clear.
example_context: You laugh at a post about forgotten birthdays, then remember your partner's birthday is tomorrow and reply with this two-stage reaction.
near_miss_context: A joke remains harmless and funny after reflection, so the serious second panel has no reversal to represent.

name: I just think they're neat
message: Use to express uncomplicated, sincere enthusiasm for a specific thing without pretending to have a sophisticated argument for it.
relational_pattern: A modest personal preference is defended by simple affection rather than analysis.
example_context: When friends ask why you keep recommending an unfashionable old game, respond that you simply think it is neat.
near_miss_context: You are comparing two products on price, durability, and warranty; the discussion calls for reasons rather than cheerful preference.

name: Kylo Ren MORE
message: Use when someone treats an already substantial result as insufficient and keeps demanding additional quantity, intensity, or features.
relational_pattern: A decision-maker repeatedly expands the request—another chart, another filter, another revision—without acknowledging the work already delivered.
example_context: Leadership reviews a complete report and responds by demanding another dashboard to summarize the first dashboard.
near_miss_context: Avoid when the first result is genuinely incomplete and one bounded revision would satisfy the original request.

name: speed screaming
message: Use as an exaggerated reaction to startling, infuriating, or overwhelmingly exciting news.
relational_pattern: A sudden stimulus produces an explosive emotional outburst far beyond a restrained response.
example_context: Your friend reveals that concert tickets sold out while you were checking out, and you answer with this scream reaction.
near_miss_context: Someone shares mildly useful scheduling information; a maximal outburst would have no comic emotional scale.

name: Swords united
message: Use when several people, groups, or ideas unite around one shared goal, enemy, belief, or interest.
relational_pattern: Separate parties form a visible coalition through a common point of agreement.
example_context: Three rival teams all oppose the proposed weekend meeting, so someone labels each sword with a team name.
near_miss_context: The participants remain divided on the central issue and merely occupy the same call; proximity is not unity.

message: Use ironically when someone treats a minor rule, moderation decision, or inconvenience as Orwellian authoritarian control.
relational_pattern: A small restriction is hyperbolically equated with totalitarian censorship or surveillance.
example_context: The server bans posting spoilers for one day, and a member replies 'literally 1984' with this image.
near_miss_context: People are discussing documented state surveillance and political repression; the reference may be literal rather than a petty overreaction.

name: Clown Makeup slander
message: Use to show someone gradually adopting increasingly foolish justifications until they have made a clown of themselves.
relational_pattern: Successive rationalizations transform confidence into visible self-humiliation.
example_context: Caption each makeup stage with a new excuse a friend gives for repeatedly texting an ex who never responds.
near_miss_context: A person changes their view after receiving solid evidence; honest reconsideration is not a clownish progression.

name: Ermahgerd Berks
message: Use to convey intense, dorky excitement, especially by rendering an enthusiastic phrase in the template's exaggerated pronunciation.
relational_pattern: Unrestrained fandom turns an ordinary announcement into gleeful, stylized speech.
example_context: Your book-club friend learns the library sale starts early and sends 'ERMAHGERD, BERKS!' to the chat.
near_miss_context: Someone politely notes that the bookstore is open; without heightened excitement, the distorted exclamation is out of place.

name: Donald Trump Mugshot
message: Use to frame someone as defiantly unbothered after being caught, charged, disciplined, or publicly criticized.
relational_pattern: Formal trouble is met with a confrontational pose rather than apology or embarrassment.
example_context: A friend receives a stern warning for organizing an unauthorized office party and posts this as their mock-defiant profile picture.
near_miss_context: A coworker is genuinely remorseful after harming someone; treating the moment as swagger would erase the apology.

name: Bugs bunny I wish all empty template
message: Use to wish a defined group a particular outcome, often warmly but sometimes with pointed sarcasm.
relational_pattern: A broad audience is addressed with one concise, targeted blessing or curse.
example_context: After support fixes a widespread outage, post 'I wish all on-call engineers a very quiet weekend' using this format.
near_miss_context: You need to explain a detailed proposal to one person; the template's group-wide wish structure cannot carry that argument.

name: Dr Evil One Million
message: Use when a sum is presented as astonishingly large even though the speaker's sense of its value is dated, naive, or comically inflated.
relational_pattern: An amount receives villainous grandeur disproportionate to its actual scale.
example_context: A manager announces a one-dollar monthly raise as though it will transform morale, and the team answers with this.
near_miss_context: A fundraiser truly reaches a record-setting amount for its field; emphasizing the total need not imply outdated valuation.

name: Help Me Obi-Wan, You're our only hope.
message: Use for a desperate appeal to the one person believed capable of solving an otherwise hopeless problem.
relational_pattern: Many options have failed, leaving a single trusted helper as the last resort.
example_context: The deployment breaks minutes before a demo, and the team tags the only colleague who understands the legacy build system with this.
near_miss_context: Several teammates are equally available and the task is routine, so portraying one person as the sole hope would overstate the stakes.

name: pie chart yes but in yellow
message: Use to mock a distinction that is technically labeled differently but amounts to the same answer or preference.
relational_pattern: A nominal alternative preserves the original choice while changing only its presentation.
example_context: A survey offers 'yes' and 'yes, but in the brand color,' so your coworker shares this to point out that dissent is impossible.
near_miss_context: A poll contains genuinely opposed options with meaningful consequences; reducing them to differently colored agreement would be inaccurate.

name: Three Buttons
message: Use when a person must choose among three incompatible, stressful, or equally tempting options.
relational_pattern: Mutually exclusive choices create visible decision paralysis and pressure.
example_context: A student can submit on time, sleep, or fix every citation—but cannot do all three—so they label the buttons accordingly.
near_miss_context: The three tasks can be completed sequentially without sacrifice, leaving no forced choice for the sweating decision-maker.

name: We Have A Hulk
message: Use when someone answers a threat or boast by revealing a decisive advantage, powerful ally, or ace in the hole.
relational_pattern: One side counters intimidation with confidence in an overwhelming resource.
example_context: A rival team brags about its new automation, and your colleague points out that your group has the person who built the underlying platform.
near_miss_context: Your side has no credible counter and is asking for mercy, so the triumphant reveal would be empty bravado.

name: Tada Will smith
message: Use to present, reveal, or point out something with theatrical pride, as if saying 'look at this.'
relational_pattern: A reveal gains humor from an extravagant presenter gesture aimed at an ordinary result.
example_context: After reorganizing one shelf, your roommate unveils it to the household group chat with this flourish.
near_miss_context: You discreetly tell a colleague about a private medical issue; a showy presentation would violate the tone and privacy.

name: Where we're going we don't need roads...
message: Use when abandoning conventional methods, constraints, or infrastructure in favor of a bold new direction.
relational_pattern: The destination is framed as so advanced or unconventional that the old path is irrelevant.
example_context: When the team replaces a chain of emailed spreadsheets with an automated workflow, announce the change with this line.
near_miss_context: You are following the standard process exactly because it remains the safest option; there is no break from convention.

name: First rule of the Fight Club
message: Use to remind a group that a subject is secret, forbidden to discuss, or governed by an unspoken rule of silence.
relational_pattern: Membership in an activity carries a primary norm against talking about it.
example_context: A colleague starts mentioning the office surprise party in the public channel, so you respond with the first-rule line.
near_miss_context: Someone reports harassment through the proper channel; invoking secrecy would suppress necessary disclosure rather than make a joke.

name: Fast Flash
message: Use when someone arrives, responds, completes a task, or disappears with implausible speed.
relational_pattern: An action's turnaround is exaggerated as superhero-level velocity.
example_context: You send a friend a restaurant link and they book the table before you finish typing the next message, so you reply with this.
near_miss_context: A contractor delivers two weeks late; a speed reaction would contradict the actual delay.

name: iceberg levels tiers
message: Use to organize a topic from familiar surface knowledge down through increasingly obscure, strange, or disturbing layers.
relational_pattern: Visible mainstream facts sit above progressively deeper insider knowledge.
example_context: A fan community maps a band's hit singles at the top and its disputed bootleg recordings at the submerged bottom.
near_miss_context: A ranked list merely orders products from cheapest to most expensive; price ranking does not imply hidden depth.

name: Happy then sad
message: Use when good news or initial excitement is immediately reversed by a disappointing qualification.
relational_pattern: A positive first beat turns negative as soon as the missing detail arrives.
example_context: Your manager says Friday is a holiday, then adds that everyone must work Saturday, and the chat posts this two-panel response.
near_miss_context: A friend's mood improves gradually over several weeks; the template expects a sharp same-moment reversal.

name: Woman Holding Kevin Hart
message: Use when someone protectively claims a person, character, idea, or object and warns critics or threats to stay away.
relational_pattern: A defender places themself between a cherished target and an outside antagonist.
example_context: When the group starts mocking your friend's harmless niche hobby, send this with yourself shielding the hobby from the critics.
near_miss_context: You are neutrally comparing two strangers with no loyalty to either one; the possessive protective stance has no role.

name: You can't if you don't
message: Use to describe a technically true but foolish loophole: an unwanted event cannot happen if you avoid its necessary precondition.
relational_pattern: A problem is 'solved' by eliminating the opportunity for the desired outcome as well.
example_context: A friend says they cannot miss a deadline if they never start the project, and you answer with this knowingly bad logic.
near_miss_context: Someone removes an unnecessary dependency and still achieves the goal; that is a sound simplification, not a self-defeating loophole.

name: The Loudest Sounds on Earth
message: Use to place an everyday sound or event at the top of an absurd scale, claiming it is louder than famously extreme examples.
relational_pattern: Comic escalation ranks a relatable nuisance beyond objectively enormous reference points.
example_context: Add 'my roommate opening chips at 2 a.m.' above rockets and volcanoes to exaggerate how impossible it is to ignore.
near_miss_context: You are documenting measured decibel levels for workplace safety; a joke ranking would undermine the factual comparison.

name: Epic Handshake Three Way
message: Use when three otherwise separate parties discover one shared belief, behavior, enemy, or interest.
relational_pattern: A three-way agreement links distinct groups through a common denominator.
example_context: Design, engineering, and support all want fewer last-minute launches, so each arm is labeled with a department.
near_miss_context: Only two sides agree while the third explicitly objects; including all three in the handshake would erase the disagreement.

name: Guy with sand in the hands of despair
message: Use for melodramatic despair when something valued is gone, slipping away, or impossible to recover.
relational_pattern: A loss is treated with theatrical, almost existential devastation.
example_context: The group learns its favorite café has removed the one affordable lunch special, and a friend posts this in exaggerated mourning.
near_miss_context: Someone is coping with a recent bereavement; the campy despair pose would be insensitive rather than relatable.

name: breaking bad smile frown
message: Use to contrast approval and disapproval of two options, or to show a reaction flipping after one crucial detail changes.
relational_pattern: A small difference in framing reverses the evaluator's expression from pleased to displeased or vice versa.
example_context: A friend likes the phrase 'team lunch' until they hear 'unpaid mandatory team lunch,' so you label the two reactions.
near_miss_context: Both proposals receive the same response and differ only cosmetically; there is no emotional switch to display.

name: Judgmental Volturi
message: Use when a person or group silently judges someone with severe, disapproving scrutiny.
relational_pattern: The target faces a collective look of condemnation rather than an explicit argument.
example_context: You admit to reheating fish in the office microwave, and the entire lunch table responds with this image.
near_miss_context: Friends listen with curiosity and reserve judgment until they know more; the tribunal-like reaction would overstate their response.

name: Smudge the cat
message: Use as a disgusted, offended, or stubbornly rejecting response to an unwanted suggestion or offering.
relational_pattern: The recipient meets what is presented with visible contempt and refusal.
example_context: Someone proposes replacing the good coffee with an instant powder, and you answer with Smudge's appalled stare.
near_miss_context: A friend offers exactly the option you requested and you accept happily; disgust would communicate the opposite.

name: Hydra
message: Use when one conspicuously foolish, weak, or unserious member stands out among otherwise formidable peers.
relational_pattern: A multi-part group contains a comic outlier whose quality falls far below the others.
example_context: Label two polished product features as the fierce heads and the crash-prone settings page as the goofy third head.
near_miss_context: All members of the group are equally competent, so singling one out as the defective head would be arbitrary.

name: slap that button
message: Use when someone accepts, selects, buys, or approves something immediately and with emphatic enthusiasm.
relational_pattern: A desirable option triggers an instant, forceful yes.
example_context: A friend asks whether the group wants an extra day off after the launch, and everyone replies with this button slap.
near_miss_context: The proposal needs careful legal review before any decision; instant approval would misrepresent the hesitation.

name: Whose Line is it Anyway
message: Use when rules, scores, roles, or stated facts are arbitrary, invented, or ultimately irrelevant to the outcome.
relational_pattern: A formal-looking system is exposed as improvised and consequence-free.
example_context: Your office awards points for meeting attendance but never uses them for anything, so the team compares it to this show.
near_miss_context: A tournament's score determines who advances under published rules; the points materially matter.

name: braveheart freedom
message: Use to celebrate breaking free from an oppressive obligation, restriction, dependency, or source of frustration.
relational_pattern: Release from constraint is proclaimed as a dramatic victory for freedom.
example_context: After the team retires a tool everyone hated maintaining, a developer posts this to celebrate liberation from it.
near_miss_context: A person refuses a reasonable safety boundary that protects others; framing that refusal as heroic freedom would distort the issue.

name: Confused Travolta
message: Use when someone looks around for a person, object, explanation, or expected activity that is conspicuously absent.
relational_pattern: Arrival at an empty or unclear scene produces visible, searching confusion.
example_context: You join the scheduled video call on time and find nobody else there, so you send this in the team chat.
near_miss_context: You know exactly where everyone is and are simply waiting for them; the searching confusion would be false.

name: Worst mistake of my life
message: Use immediately after a bad choice backfires, especially when the regret is obvious and the consequences are already chasing you.
relational_pattern: A voluntary decision is followed by instant recognition that it was disastrously wrong.
example_context: Seconds after volunteering to coordinate the reunion, fifty relatives begin sending conflicting requests, and you post this.
near_miss_context: An unavoidable accident happens despite a careful decision; calling it your mistake would assign responsibility inaccurately.

name: Amateurs
message: Use to one-up a displayed mistake, failure, or extreme behavior by revealing an even more spectacular version.
relational_pattern: A supposedly notable example is dismissed as amateur beside the speaker's superior level of chaos or failure.
example_context: A friend says they missed one deadline, and you reply with the time you missed an entire registration window: 'Amateurs.'
near_miss_context: Someone asks a beginner for help learning a skill; belittling them offers no humorous escalation and is needlessly hostile.

name: Guy talking to girl in club
message: Use for an unwanted, one-sided explanation delivered at length to someone who is visibly trapped or uninterested.
relational_pattern: One person enthusiastically lectures while the listener endures the interaction without engagement.
example_context: Caption the speaker as you explaining your fantasy-league strategy and the listener as the friend who only asked what time dinner starts.
near_miss_context: Both friends eagerly trade stories and ask follow-up questions; mutual conversation is not the template's imbalance.

name: I WANT YOU
message: Use as a direct recruitment or call to action aimed at the viewer or a specifically named person.
relational_pattern: An authority figure singles out the audience as the person needed for a mission or responsibility.
example_context: The volunteer group still needs one event photographer, so its organizer posts this with 'I want you to bring a camera.'
near_miss_context: A general announcement provides information without asking anyone to act; the pointed recruitment gesture would add a demand.

name: Trumpet Boy
message: Use when a loud, persistent person or thing keeps intruding on someone who wants to be left alone.
relational_pattern: An oblivious provocateur repeatedly directs noise at an increasingly irritated target.
example_context: Label the trumpet player 'calendar reminders' and the girl 'me trying to enjoy Sunday evening.'
near_miss_context: A friend plays music after everyone enthusiastically asks for it; welcomed entertainment lacks the unwanted provocation.

name: Stop it, Patrick! You're Scaring Him!
message: Use when one person reveals increasingly intense, unsettling, or technical information until another becomes frightened or overwhelmed.
relational_pattern: Escalating disclosure disturbs an audience while a bystander urges the speaker to stop.
example_context: A developer explains each new consequence of the old billing bug to a nervous product manager, and a teammate posts this.
near_miss_context: The explanation reassures the listener and reduces their concern at every step; the fear escalation is absent.

name: Manly Handshake
message: Use to show two people, groups, or concepts bonding over a shared trait, deal, victory, or point of agreement.
relational_pattern: Distinct sides meet in the middle through one strongly shared connection.
example_context: Label the arms 'remote workers' and 'office workers' and the handshake 'muting pointless notifications.'
near_miss_context: The two groups remain opposed on the labeled issue, so a handshake would falsely suggest common ground.

name: jesus watcha doin
message: Use when someone's questionable behavior seems to be observed by a moral authority, conscience, or disapproving presence.
relational_pattern: A private misdeed becomes awkward because judgment appears to be peeking in.
example_context: Your friend admits using the shared streaming password after promising not to, and you respond with Jesus watching from the edge.
near_miss_context: A person openly performs a generous act they have no reason to hide; implied moral suspicion would not fit.

name: Walter White Breaks Down
message: Use for a complete emotional collapse when bad news, loss, guilt, or accumulated pressure finally becomes unbearable.
relational_pattern: Composure gives way to raw distress after the person reaches a breaking point.
example_context: After weeks of revisions, a client asks the team to restore the very first draft, and the designer replies with this breakdown.
near_miss_context: Someone is mildly annoyed by a typo and fixes it in seconds; the scale is far below a genuine collapse.

name: Plane flying from explosions
message: Use when someone escapes, departs, or carries on looking composed while chaos erupts behind them.
relational_pattern: A successful exit is contrasted with the disaster left in its wake.
example_context: A contractor submits the final files and begins vacation just as the client starts a chaotic revision thread, prompting this reaction.
near_miss_context: A colleague stays behind to manage the emergency and accepts responsibility; the carefree getaway framing would misstate their role.

name: Scout opening the fridge
message: Use for repeatedly checking a place despite already knowing that nothing new or useful will be there.
relational_pattern: Habit and faint hope drive another pointless inspection of an unchanged source.
example_context: You refresh an empty inbox five seconds after the last refresh and send this to acknowledge the compulsion.
near_miss_context: A notification confirms that a requested message has arrived; checking now has new information and is not futile repetition.

name: Deep Thoughts
message: Use for mock-philosophical reflection on a question that sounds profound but is often trivial, absurd, or obvious.
relational_pattern: An everyday observation is elevated into exaggerated intellectual contemplation.
example_context: A friend wonders whether a meeting about reducing meetings should count as another meeting and posts this as a deep thought.
near_miss_context: A team is carefully analyzing a difficult ethical decision with real consequences; treating it as faux wisdom could trivialize the work.

name: Omni Man blocks punch
message: Use when an attack, criticism, challenge, or supposed advantage is stopped effortlessly by someone far stronger.
relational_pattern: A threatening move proves powerless against an unbothered superior opponent.
example_context: A competitor boasts that its new feature will crush your product, but it merely copies a capability your team shipped years ago; reply with this block.
near_miss_context: The challenge causes serious damage and forces a desperate recovery, so effortless invulnerability would be inaccurate.

name: Edna Mode No Capes
message: Use to impose an emphatic, categorical ban on a tempting option because its recurring downside is too dangerous or impractical.
relational_pattern: Past failures turn a design preference into a memorable safety rule with no exceptions.
example_context: After another launch fails because of a Friday release, the team adopts 'No Friday deploys!' and posts this.
near_miss_context: A harmless stylistic preference is still under open discussion; invoking a disaster-backed absolute would overstate the evidence.

name: Inception
message: Use when an idea, story, joke, or system contains one layer nested inside another, often recursively.
relational_pattern: A concept repeats within itself or descends through multiple embedded levels.
example_context: Your team schedules a meeting to plan the agenda for another planning meeting, and someone labels it meeting inception.
near_miss_context: Two unrelated tasks happen side by side without one containing the other; mere complexity is not nesting.

name: Why you no
message: Use as a frustrated demand asking why someone will not perform an obvious, desired, or repeatedly requested action.
relational_pattern: A simple unmet expectation is expressed through exaggerated broken-grammar exasperation.
example_context: After the printer rejects the same valid file again, message the office chat with 'Why you no print?'
near_miss_context: You are asking a nuanced question that requires a careful explanation; the rage-comic demand would sound dismissive.

name: Pepe Silvia
message: Use when someone has built an elaborate theory from scattered details and explains the supposed connections with frantic certainty.
relational_pattern: Obsessive investigation turns weak or tangled evidence into a sprawling conspiracy map.
example_context: A coworker links meeting times, coffee orders, and calendar colors to prove a secret reorganization is coming, so the team posts this.
near_miss_context: An auditor presents a short, documented chain of evidence; rigorously supported findings are not conspiracy-board mania.

name: Are you winning son blank template
message: Use for a parent's earnest but slightly awkward attempt to understand or support a child's hobby, game, or online activity.
relational_pattern: Generational distance is bridged by a simple check-in whose wording may miss the activity's real point.
example_context: Your dad texts 'are you winning?' during a long coding competition, and you share this affectionately with your teammates.
near_miss_context: A manager demands performance metrics from an employee; the power dynamic is evaluation, not parental support.

name: Four Naan Jeremy? Four? That's insane
message: Use to express incredulity that someone chose, consumed, bought, or requested an excessive number of one thing.
relational_pattern: A surprisingly large quantity is repeated back as evidence that the person has gone too far.
example_context: A friend orders four desserts for themselves, and the table responds, 'Four? That's insane,' with this format.
near_miss_context: Four batteries are exactly what the device requires; the quantity is functional rather than comically excessive.

name: rick and morty-extra steps
message: Use when a complicated process is revealed to be a familiar simple activity with unnecessary intermediaries.
relational_pattern: Needless procedure disguises an ordinary result as innovation or sophistication.
example_context: A startup describes ordering lunch through three tokens and a chatbot, and your friend observes that it is delivery with extra steps.
near_miss_context: The additional stages provide essential verification and prevent costly errors; they are not decorative complexity.

name: Grim Reaper Claw Machine
message: Use when fate, danger, layoffs, illness, or another grim force appears to be selecting its next target from a group.
relational_pattern: An impersonal threat repeatedly claims members while the survivors wait to see who is chosen next.
example_context: After a bug reaches a different service every day, engineers label the claw 'the incident' and the prizes with team names.
near_miss_context: A transparent rotation assigns routine duties fairly; random ominous victim selection would mischaracterize the process.

name: DBZ FUSION
message: Use when two people, traits, products, or ideas combine to create a hybrid that contains recognizable parts of both.
relational_pattern: Separate identities merge into a single composite with amplified or mixed qualities.
example_context: A friend describes the new café as a library fused with a nightclub, so you label each fighter with one half of the concept.
near_miss_context: One product simply replaces another without retaining any of its features; substitution is not fusion.

name: Metronome
message: Use when someone or something repeatedly swings between two opposite moods, opinions, states, or choices.
relational_pattern: Rapid alternation prevents a stable position from lasting.
example_context: Your group chat changes from 'cancel the trip' to 'book it now' every hour, so you label each side of the metronome.
near_miss_context: A person makes one considered change and then stays consistent; a single transition is not oscillation.

name: What's on your mind?
message: Use to reveal the one thought, obsession, worry, or oddly specific subject occupying someone's mind beneath a calm exterior.
relational_pattern: An outwardly ordinary person is contrasted with the dominant idea inside their head.
example_context: During dinner you keep thinking about whether you locked the office, so you label the skull with that intrusive concern.
near_miss_context: A friend openly tells everyone exactly what they are considering; there is no hidden inner thought to expose.

name: the office bankruptcy
message: Use when someone believes merely declaring a status or outcome will make it legally or practically true.
relational_pattern: A performative announcement is mistaken for the real process needed to produce its result.
example_context: A teammate says 'I declare this project finished' while half the checklist is open, and the group responds with this.
near_miss_context: An authorized official completes the required procedure and then announces the result; the declaration has real force.

name: panic toad
message: Use as a compact visual for sudden panic, alarm, or horrified realization.
relational_pattern: A new fact instantly converts calm into wide-eyed distress.
example_context: You remember at 11:58 p.m. that an assignment is due at midnight and send this to your study group.
near_miss_context: Someone calmly prepares for a known deadline over several days; the abrupt panic reaction would exaggerate their state.

name: Are you two friends?
message: Use when two people give incompatible answers about whether they are friends, exposing a one-sided or awkward relationship.
relational_pattern: One person claims closeness while the other simultaneously denies it.
example_context: Two coworkers are asked whether they are best friends; one says yes and the other says no, so the team recreates this exchange.
near_miss_context: Both people consistently describe the relationship the same way; there is no mismatch for the split answer.

name: Forever alone
message: Use for self-deprecating loneliness, romantic exclusion, or the feeling that everyone else has companionship.
relational_pattern: The speaker casts themself as the solitary outsider to other people's connections.
example_context: Your friends pair off for a couples' quiz and you are the only unpaired guest, so you send this to the chat.
near_miss_context: You intentionally choose a quiet evening alone and feel content; solitude without sadness is not forever-alone despair.

name: One please
message: Use when a shown item, person, experience, or benefit looks so desirable that someone immediately requests one for themself.
relational_pattern: Seeing an appealing example triggers a concise order for the same thing.
example_context: A friend shares a photo of their company-issued nap pod, and you reply 'one please' to express envy.
near_miss_context: You are negotiating the detailed specifications and quantity of a purchase; the minimal reaction cannot communicate those requirements.

name: Finally, inner peace.
message: Use when a long-running irritation, uncertainty, or conflict is finally resolved and calm returns.
relational_pattern: Removal of a persistent disturbance produces satisfying mental quiet.
example_context: After the smoke alarm's low-battery chirp is finally fixed, your household chat posts this in relief.
near_miss_context: The underlying problem remains active and everyone is merely ignoring it; avoidance is not genuine resolution.

name: I am the Senate
message: Use when one person arrogantly claims to embody an institution, group, rule-making body, or all legitimate authority.
relational_pattern: Individual power erases the distinction between the leader and the system meant to constrain them.
example_context: The club president rejects a vote by saying their opinion is the club's opinion, prompting members to post this.
near_miss_context: A spokesperson accurately reports a decision made through the group's normal vote; representation is not monopolized authority.

name: So You Agree
message: Use to seize on someone's admission and show that it supports the conclusion they were resisting.
relational_pattern: A question elicits agreement that exposes a contradiction or concedes the speaker's premise.
example_context: A friend insists meetings are useful but admits they cancel every meeting without an agenda; reply, 'So you agree—agendas matter.'
near_miss_context: The other person explicitly rejects your premise, so claiming agreement would fabricate a concession.

name: Sonic Says
message: Use to deliver a mock public-service lesson, moral, warning, or rule in the style of an educational character segment.
relational_pattern: A simple piece of advice is framed as an authoritative after-school message.
example_context: After a friend loses work by closing an unsaved file, post 'Sonic says: save before you quit.'
near_miss_context: The topic requires nuanced professional guidance with important exceptions; a jokey one-line lesson would oversimplify it.

name: All My Homies Love
message: Use to show that an entire friend group enthusiastically approves of, supports, or enjoys the same person or thing.
relational_pattern: Collective loyalty turns a preference into a shared group identity.
example_context: Your friends unanimously praise the colleague who always brings snacks, so you caption the group 'All my homies love Maya.'
near_miss_context: The group is split and several members dislike the subject; claiming universal affection would erase the disagreement.

name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs

name: worship the lord
message: Use when someone treats a person, object, brand, or idea with absurdly reverent devotion.

near_miss_context: A person is sincerely discussing their religious practice; using an ironic worship template may be disrespectful and unclear.

name: My precious Gollum

name: I WANT PICTURES OF SPIDERMAN

name: here's johnny
message: Use for a sudden, forceful, or uninvited entrance that startles people already inside a conversation or space.

name: Dafuq did I just read
message: Use after reading something so incoherent, bizarre, offensive, or mentally taxing that ordinary confusion is insufficient.

example_context: A friend forwards a paragraph whose argument contradicts itself in every sentence, and you respond with this reaction.
near_miss_context: The document is clear but you disagree with its conclusion; disagreement alone is not bewilderment at the text itself.

name: HOMER BUSH

name: gondor calls for aid

name: Nobody Expects the Spanish Inquisition Monty Python
message: Use when an unexpected person, event, demand, or complication abruptly interrupts an otherwise ordinary situation.
relational_pattern: Surprise itself is the joke: the audience could not reasonably anticipate the intervention.

near_miss_context: The agenda clearly announced the guest weeks ago; calling the arrival unexpected would ignore shared notice.

name: Forest Gump Running
message: Use when someone keeps going far beyond the expected stopping point, or abruptly decides to run away from the situation altogether.

name: Captain america elevator
message: Use when people sharing a confined setting realize a confrontation is imminent and tension spikes before anyone acts.

near_miss_context: The passengers are relaxed strangers making small talk; an impending fight would invent tension that is not there.

name: This Little Manuever is Gonna Cost us 51 Years
message: Use when a clever-looking action, shortcut, or tradeoff succeeds only by imposing a comically enormous long-term cost.

near_miss_context: A maneuver saves time now without creating future debt; there is no delayed price to exaggerate.

name: Hans Landa hiding enemies of the state
message: Use for a tense interrogation in which someone must conceal a secret, protect another person, or survive an authority figure's probing questions.

name: Professor Farnsworth Good News Everyone
message: Use to announce news with upbeat confidence when the information is dubious, inconvenient, or likely to be bad for the audience.
relational_pattern: Cheerful framing clashes with the unwelcome substance of the announcement.

near_miss_context: You are sharing genuinely welcome news with no catch or irony; the ominous cheerfulness may imply a hidden downside.

name: spongebob wanna see me do it again
message: Use when someone performs an impressive, reckless, annoying, or absurd feat and immediately offers to repeat it.
relational_pattern: A completed action becomes a boast through effortless, eager repetition.
example_context: After finding one bug in seconds, a tester finds another identical one and asks the developers, 'Wanna see me do it again?'
near_miss_context: A person fails once and is reluctant to retry; the template requires confidence and repeatability rather than hesitant recovery.

name: Straining kid
message: Use when a simple task, decision, or act of self-control requires visibly disproportionate effort.
relational_pattern: Minor resistance is portrayed as an exhausting full-body struggle.
example_context: You try not to correct a harmless typo in a casual group chat and send this to show the effort of staying silent.
near_miss_context: A genuinely strenuous emergency rescue demands major exertion; the humor depends on effort being excessive for the task.

name: Squidward competition
message: Use when entering a competition only to discover that the opponent is uniquely dominant at the exact skill being tested.
relational_pattern: Hope collapses because the matchup favors an unbeatable specialist.
example_context: You enter a trivia round about your coworker's hometown and learn that coworker is your opponent, so you post this.
near_miss_context: The opponent is inexperienced and the contest is evenly matched; doomed recognition would be premature.

name: "We did it, Patrick! We saved the City!"
message: Use to celebrate a supposed success when the attempted solution has actually caused enormous damage or made the problem worse.
relational_pattern: Self-congratulation ignores the destruction produced by the 'rescue.'
example_context: After removing one spam post by accidentally deleting the entire forum, an admin jokes, 'We did it—we saved the community.'
near_miss_context: A careful fix solves the problem without collateral harm; ironic failure-celebration would be undeserved.

name: Dodge chad vs virgin
message: Use to contrast an admired, powerful, or confident version of something with a weaker, awkward, or inferior counterpart.

near_miss_context: The two choices have balanced strengths and neither is clearly framed as superior; the caricature would force a false hierarchy.

name: I'm awake, but at what cost?
message: Use when achieving wakefulness required so little sleep or such unpleasant effort that being awake feels like a bad bargain.

example_context: After three coffees get you through an early meeting following two hours of sleep, send this to your team.
near_miss_context: You wake naturally after a full night's rest and feel refreshed; there is no painful tradeoff.

name: Borat i go to america
message: Use when announcing a trip, move, or visit with conspicuous excitement and slightly naive confidence.
relational_pattern: Eager arrival: an outsider enthusiastically sets off for an unfamiliar destination and imagines the adventure ahead.
example_context: A friend gets approval for their first international conference and posts 'I go to Berlin' before booking anything else.
near_miss_context: Avoid for an ordinary commute to a familiar office; the format needs novelty, travel, and outsized anticipation.

name: Gunna Writes In Fire Meme
message: Use to praise writing, music, an argument, or creative work as exceptionally good—as though the creator is producing fire.

example_context: A friend delivers a devastatingly funny comeback in the group chat, and you reply that they are writing in fire.
near_miss_context: The message is careless and unconvincing; using the template sincerely would praise work you mean to criticize.

name: Smash Bros.
message: Use to announce that a new participant, faction, idea, or complication has dramatically entered an ongoing conflict.

near_miss_context: One side quietly leaves and nobody new enters; the battlefield has shrunk rather than gained a participant.

name: Mean Girls - Stop Trying to Make Fetch Happen
message: Use to tell someone to stop forcing a phrase, trend, plan, nickname, or idea that plainly is not catching on.

example_context: A coworker uses the same awkward project nickname in every meeting despite nobody adopting it, so the team sends this.
near_miss_context: A new term has spread organically and everyone already uses it; declaring it impossible would lag behind reality.

name: Change My Mind (tilt-corrected)
message: Use to state a debatable opinion with conspicuous confidence and invite others to challenge it.
relational_pattern: A provocative claim is presented as the starting position for public argument, not as a surrendered belief.
example_context: Post 'Breakfast food is better at dinner—change my mind' to start a playful debate among friends.
near_miss_context: You have already reconsidered after new evidence and want to announce your updated view; the template instead signals current conviction.

name: Show me the money
message: Use when someone demands concrete payment, revenue, funding, or financial proof instead of promises and enthusiasm.
relational_pattern: Commitment is made conditional on seeing real money rather than projections or praise.
example_context: A client offers exposure instead of a fee, and the freelancer replies with this to insist on actual compensation.
near_miss_context: A volunteer explicitly agreed to an unpaid community role; introducing a payment ultimatum changes the arrangement.

name: Kramer, what's going on in there
message: Use when alarming, bizarre, or chaotic activity is clearly happening nearby but remains hidden from view.
relational_pattern: An observer confronts someone at the boundary of a concealed disturbance and demands an explanation.
example_context: Your neighbors' renovation produces a crash followed by cheering, so you message a friend with this reaction.
near_miss_context: You can see the routine activity clearly and already know its cause; there is no mysterious 'in there' to question.

name: Black guy disappearing
message: Use when someone withdraws or vanishes as soon as a situation becomes awkward, demanding, dangerous, or inconvenient.
relational_pattern: Presence fades in stages once staying would require uncomfortable involvement.
example_context: The group asks who wants to write the meeting notes, and the most talkative member suddenly stops replying; post this.
near_miss_context: A friend explains in advance that they must leave for an appointment; a planned departure is not evasive disappearance.

name: crying michael jordan
message: Use to attach conspicuous sadness or humiliation to a person, team, brand, or idea that has just lost or failed.
relational_pattern: A defeat is personalized by overlaying the iconic crying expression on its subject.

near_miss_context: Someone shares a serious private grief; turning it into a sports-style humiliation gag would be cruel.

name: Michael Jackson popcorn gif
message: Use when watching drama, conflict, gossip, or a public meltdown unfold from the sidelines for entertainment.
relational_pattern: A spectator consumes the escalating spectacle without intervening.
example_context: Two rival fan groups begin arguing under a harmless post, and you send the popcorn reaction to a friend following the thread.
near_miss_context: A dangerous dispute requires you to help or call support; passive entertainment would be irresponsible.

name: Joey Repeat After Me
message: Use when patient instruction repeatedly fails because the learner misstates, misunderstands, or cannot reproduce a simple point.
relational_pattern: A teacher breaks a message into smaller pieces while the other person keeps producing the wrong result.
example_context: You coach a friend through pronouncing a new colleague's name, but each attempt gets further away, so you share this exchange.
near_miss_context: The learner repeats the phrase correctly on the first try; there is no escalating communication failure.

name: Peter Parker Reading Book & Crying
message: Use when reading reveals an emotionally painful, tragic, or deeply disappointing fact.
relational_pattern: New written information turns concentration into visible heartbreak.
example_context: You open the event email and discover your favorite speaker cancelled, then reply with Peter Parker reading through tears.
near_miss_context: The text is merely confusing and produces no sadness; a bewildered-reading reaction would fit better.

name: Wants to know your location
message: Use when a named person, organization, or character would urgently seek someone out after hearing a provocative claim or offense.

near_miss_context: A company requests an address solely to deliver an order; literal logistics lack the implied confrontation.

name: Get a Load of this Guy
message: Use to invite others to notice and ridicule someone who has said or done something foolish, boastful, or embarrassing.
relational_pattern: A target is publicly presented as an object of amused disbelief.
